newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yamaichi in scandal spolight as penalties awaited.
newsitem.headline: Yamaichi in scandal spolight as penalties awaited.

text.p: Japan's high-profile racketeer payoff scandal ensnared another big brokerage on Wednesday as prosecutors raided Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd for evidence of illegal deals amid signs the affair could widen still further.

A government source told reporters that Yamaichi had "generally" admitted to illegally paying compensation for losses incurred by a corporate client linked to Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal which has already entangled Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB), one of the nation's biggest banks.

On Wednesday, some 200 investigators from the prosecutors office and the government watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), raided offices of Yamaichi -- one of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages -- for evidence of the illegal deals.
The move came as authorities finalised penalties against Nomura and DKB for their involvement in the scandal. The penalties are likely to be announced later on Wednesday.
Prosecutors told reporters they suspected Yamaichi had paid 79 million yen ($669,000) to Koike.

Domestic media said Yamaichi allegedly made the payments in 1995 to obtain Koike's help in ensuring that its annual shareholders' meeting went smoothly. Yamaichi said in a statement that it would cooperate with the investigation but would not comment on whether the allegations were true.

More than a dozen people have already been arrested in the affair, which coincides with the start of "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition and global standards into Japan's long-sheltered financial sector.

Authorities are keen to be seen as tough on such misdeeds as they push forward with deregulation, and penalties against Nomura and DKB are likely to be the harshest ever, including suspension of some key business for as long as five months.
But analysts said the two huge financial institutions were likely to survive the blow and could even end up in better shape following management shakeups prompted by the scandal.

Domestic media also said on Wednesday that Tokyo prosecutors appeared to have launched investigations into the other two of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages, Daiwa Securities Co Ltd and Nikko Securities Co Ltd, in connection with the affair.
A Daiwa spokesman, however, denied the media reports of illicit deals and Nikko said it did not think it had conducted any illegal transactions.

Yamaichi's shares were down 20 yen to 281 yen at midday. Nomura was down 10 yen to 1,570 yen, Nikko eased 15 yen to 676 yen and Daiwa dropped 34 yen to 831 yen. But DKB shares rose 20 yen to 1,520 yen.
Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1983, but many companies have found it tough to cut off underworld ties.

Sokaiya buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices. Alternatively, they are sometimes employed by firms to quash questions from legitimate shareholders at annual meetings.
On Tuesday, the Finance Ministry said it had reprimanded two of its officials who conducted inspections of DKB for accepting favours from officials of the scandal-tainted firm.
The ministry said the acts had not affected the results of inspections but it was necessary to maintain discipline so that inspections would not lose credibility.

The ministry came under fire when DKB's role in the scandal broke for failing to discover the dubious deals, although officials said it was virtually impossible to uncover what banks chose to hide. ($1=118 yen)
